text: A SAFETYNET briefing room. Director Netherton stands at the head of the table. Beside him, Nightshade has three monitors of access logs open.
Agent 0x00. This one is close to home in a way I dislike. Someone inside a Home Office contractor is handing ENTROPY the crown jewels.
I have brought Nightshade in because catching a mole is precisely his trade. Learn from him. HaX will run you on the ground.
Task Force Null is three people and a whiteboard so far. Every cell we've hit bought something. This time it's bought a person. I want to know how.
That is what you are going to tell me.
Insiders are hard to catch because they never have to break in. They're already trusted.
So you hunt the pattern. Access a little too broad, hours a little too odd.
And the calm of someone who's decided the rules don't apply to them. Find whose behaviour stopped matching their story.
Sound advice. HaX -- the detail.
Quantum Dynamics Corporation, on a science park outside Cambridge. Quantum-safe cryptography, under contract to the Home Office.
Someone on the inside is stealing it.
Project Heisenberg. Quantum-safe key material for the national emergency dispatch network. The system that routes nine-nine-nine calls.
Seventy-three per cent of the package is already staged to go. The rest goes out within four hours unless we stop it.
Lattice-based key exchange parameters. The production candidate set.
And the rollout schedule: cutover dates, region by region, with the key-rotation windows.
Everything ENTROPY needs to own the dispatch network the day it goes live.
No foreign buyer. ENTROPY's Insider Threat Initiative is taking it and keeping it.
Hold the keys during a rotation window and you can force the network onto a degraded routing path.
Every ambulance, fire and police call through it runs six to eleven minutes slower.
Early modelling: thirty to forty-five excess civilian deaths in the first rollout wave.
Cardiac arrests. Strokes. Structure fires. The calls where minutes decide it.
Three things, then.
One. Find the insider. QDC's security chief has it down to eight people in the cryptography division.
Their access is real, so nothing will look like a break-in.
Look at the edges. A badge at an odd hour. Money that doesn't add up. Someone who's changed.
And don't take anyone's hunch for proof. Patricia's included.
Two. Build the case. Enough for the police to act on when we pass it over anonymously, or enough to turn them.
ENTROPY's Insider Threat Initiative runs on a recruiter, working behind a headhunting firm.
Twenty-three active placements. Forty-seven more targets under evaluation.
Turn this insider into a double agent, and we map the lot.
Three. Stop the final upload. The rotation windows are in that last part, and they stay in the building.
You're going in as an external security consultant.
Your kit goes in with you. Picks, the cloner, and the print kit you brought back from Albion. Auditors carry odd bags; nobody looks.
Still no PIN cracker. The lab isn't finished with it.
Chief Security Officer Patricia Morgan is expecting you. Ex-military police, fifteen years at the National Crime Agency. She called us in.
She'll get you in. The CEO would rather none of it was happening, and wants it kept quiet.
Dr Ruth Halloran leads the cryptography team. Brilliant scientist, protective of her people.
Owen Gallagher, IT. He holds the spare cards and the server-room password, and he logs who gets them.
Lisa Park in marketing notices things. Office gossip, mostly. Some of it useful.
We can't get you a staff badge, so you'll be borrowing access on site. Owen in IT is your best bet.
There's a drop-site terminal in the server room. Secure channel for whatever you pull off their systems.
Their research portal runs Bludit. Whatever the insider is staging goes through that box.
Then find the login. Four flags on that server. I want them all.
Last thing. How are you going to play it?
Good. Write it all down. The police will want every page.
Thirty to forty-five lives ride on that upload. Keep the number with you.
Just watch the clock while you're at it.
I'm on the phone throughout. Call with what you find. Flags go in the drop-site.
Don't decide the insider's story until you've seen all of it.
And remember who ENTROPY goes looking for.
Good luck, Agent.
Quantum Dynamics. Wednesday afternoon, half past four.
The final upload goes tonight. You have four hours.
Patricia Morgan's expecting you. Go.
SAFETYNET headquarters, Thursday, nine o'clock. HaX has your report up on the screen.
Let's go through it.
You stopped the upload. The file behind it is thin. The police will get what we send them, and it won't be much.
QDC's readiness review passed. Nobody asked who told Patricia to stop looking.
You said you'd be methodical. The file's thinner than that promise.
The final upload stopped at ninety-seven per cent. The key material left in pieces over six weeks. The rotation windows were in the last of it, and they never went.
Without those, what they have is a very expensive paperweight.
Three per cent. I'd rather not do that again.
Every locked door in that building, you opened on someone else's trust. A colleague's badge, a colleague's password, his thumbprint.
In the logs, that looks exactly like an insider. It's why nobody saw him.
Old software with a known flaw nobody had patched, and an admin login in a lockbox whose code was Owen's badge number.
Once you were in, one account was allowed to run far more than its job needed. That's how you reached the Architect's sign-off.
Owen's, on paper. One sysadmin, after the budget cuts. The CEO wanted a clean audit more than a safe one.
You found him by what he did. Next time, look for the signs that come before.
You held him and Patricia called the police. He hasn't said a word to them or to us.
Our evidence reached them without our name on it. What a court gives him is out of our hands.
Elena's treatment is unfunded. She has months, maybe. Sofia and Miguel may watch that with their father on remand.
They do. For everyone near him.
Without him, we're blind on the Initiative. The placements carry on, and so does TalentStack's recruiting.
The Architect's authorisation is the part I keep coming back to. A casualty projection, reviewed, and filed as an acceptable cost.
The same hand.
Ransomware Incorporated. Zero Day Syndicate. Critical Mass. Now the Insider Threat Initiative.
The cells share suppliers, targets and a signature. The Architect runs them like a business.
And pays them like one. The Initiative got eight hundred and forty-seven thousand dollars for this job alone.
The authorisation goes up on Task Force Null's wall, with every other directive we've pulled off a cell.
Somebody pays the Architect, too. Next, we follow the money.
Ask me in a year.
Go home. Take the rest of the day.
The people who'd have waited too long for that ambulance will never know your name. But they're alive.
That's everything.
